content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with 0.85 confidence. How hard a new task was depended on how closely its outputs matched the trained task, not on how many new rules it had.

**Design:** I trained the learner on one task, L1-S1-M1. I then tested tasks where the two hypotheses predict different results. "Similarity" here is the fraction of inputs on which a task gives the same response as L1-S1-M1, as reported by `compare`.

| Test task | New rules | Similarity | Mean examples to criterion (n) |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M4 | 1 | 0.75 | ~17 (7) |
| L3-S1-M1 | 1 | 0 | ~33 (5) |
| L1-S1-M3 | 1 | 0 | ~39 (7) |
| L1-S4-M4 | 2 | 0.56 | ~34 (5) |
| L4-S3-M3 | 3 | 0 | ~40 (5) |
| L3-S1-M4 | 2 | 0 | ~48 (5) |

**What the results show:**
- **Same number of new rules, very different cost:** the three tasks with one new rule ranged from about 17 to 39 examples, and the cheapest was the one most similar to the trained task. A part-based learner would treat them about the same.
- **More new rules didn't cost more:** the task with three new rules (about 40) was no harder than the dissimilar tasks with one new rule.
- **M4 isn't an easy rule on its own:** L3-S1-M4 contains M4 but shares no responses with the trained task, and it was the hardest task tested (about 48).

**Why not higher confidence:**
- Single tests were very noisy: L1-S1-M4 alone ranged from 1 to 25 examples.
- The learner's real similarity measure is hidden. I used response overlap as a stand-in for it.

The difference between the similar and dissimilar one-new-rule tasks is about 20 examples, roughly four standard errors, so the main result is unlikely to be noise. I used 35 of the 60 budget points (1 training, 34 tests).
